prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

I am not saying “mark my words,”as the thief says early each winter.He leaves nothing of value. He too wants.A brute with language, he has a fondnessfor preaching. I am bathed to luster.Memories move musically through my bones.He sings above, vaults off a horse with feignedkindness, lands so fancy. Letting go of this, sitting with tropical leaves the size of menin a terrarium, I am beautiful. He means well, admonishing women. He is lucky with the show of crankiness.What does it mean to let go the envy?I sometimes hope stars don’t spread themselvesover New York’s lights. Performing for himself,glasses glittering, he reads stories of poverty,claims them all as his own. Here in Colorado irises of all colors unfoldoutwards to the half-hidden sun. On the cracked cement, chilly before rain, I see perpetual beginnings. I’m going to forget him:lock him in a box in my head,lock him in the haunt of violins, let go what’s his in the hurl of breath of my groans.

prompts.L3:
Please expand the following bullet points into a complete, well-structured text:

- The speaker reflects on a thief-like man who desires attention and preaches despite leaving nothing of value.
- The speaker contrasts painful memories of him with moments of beauty, nature, and self-recognition.
- The man is portrayed as performative and appropriative, claiming stories of poverty as his own.
- Images of Colorado irises, rain, and cracked cement suggest renewal and perpetual beginnings.
- The speaker resolves to forget him by mentally locking him away and letting go of his influence.
prompts.L4:
Please expand the following two-sentence summary into a complete text:

The poem explores the speaker’s struggle to release envy and resentment toward a performative, self-important man by moving through memory, vivid natural imagery, and acts of imaginative containment. It finds renewal in choosing to forget and mentally “lock” him away, suggesting that letting go restores beauty, agency, and the possibility of perpetual beginnings.
prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: Memories, Letting, What

outputs.L1:
I am not saying, “Mark my words,” as the thief says early each winter.  
He leaves nothing of value. He, too, wants.  
A brute with language, he has a fondness for preaching.  
I am bathed to luster.  
Memories move musically through my bones.  
He sings above, vaults off a horse with feigned kindness,  
lands so fancy. Letting go of this,  
sitting with tropical leaves the size of men in a terrarium,  
I am beautiful. He means well, admonishing women.  
He is lucky with the show of crankiness.  
What does it mean to let go the envy?  
I sometimes hope stars don’t spread themselves  
over New York’s lights. Performing for himself,  
glasses glittering, he reads stories of poverty,  
claims them all as his own. Here in Colorado,  
irises of all colors unfold outwards  
to the half-hidden sun. On the cracked cement,  
chilly before rain, I see perpetual beginnings.  
I’m going to forget him:  
lock him in a box in my head,  
lock him in the haunt of violins,  
let go what’s his in the hurl of breath of my groans.
outputs.L2:
I’m not declaring, “remember this,” the way the thief does at the start of every winter.  
He takes away anything worthwhile; he is needy too.  
A coarse creature armed with words, he likes to sermonize.  
I have been washed until I shine.  
Recollections pass through my skeleton like music.  
Above me he sings, springs from a horse with counterfeit gentleness,  
and comes down with theatrical grace.  

Releasing this, resting among tropical leaves as large as human bodies  
inside a glass enclosure, I find myself lovely.  
He believes his intentions are good while he scolds women.  
His irritable performance serves him well.  
What is it to surrender jealousy?  
At times I wish the stars would not scatter their brightness  
across the lights of New York.  

Putting on a show only for himself,  
his spectacles flashing, he recites tales about poverty  
and insists every one belongs to him.  
Here in Colorado, irises in every shade open  
toward the sun that is partly concealed.  
On the broken concrete, cold before the rain arrives,  
I notice beginnings that never end.  

I will erase him:  
shut him inside a box within my mind,  
seal him into the ghostly echo of violins,  
and release whatever belongs to him  
in the thrown breath of my moans.
outputs.L3:
The speaker reflects on a man who is figured almost like a thief: someone who craves attention, performs importance, and speaks as if he has wisdom to offer, yet ultimately leaves behind nothing of real value. He is remembered as a preacher-like presence, eager to occupy space and claim authority, but his words and actions feel empty. Rather than offering truth, care, or meaning, he seems to take from others—attention, stories, emotional energy—without giving anything lasting in return.

Against these painful memories, the speaker sets images of beauty, nature, and self-recognition. The memory of the man is not allowed to dominate the entire emotional landscape. Instead, it is contrasted with moments that feel alive and restorative: flowers, rain, the natural world, and the speaker’s own awareness of self. These images suggest that even after harm or disappointment, there remains a world beyond him—one capable of offering clarity, renewal, and tenderness.

The man is portrayed as deeply performative. He appears to adopt poses, roles, and narratives in order to seem more profound or authentic than he is. In particular, he appropriates stories of poverty and hardship, claiming them as though they belong to him. This makes his preaching even more hollow, because it is built not on genuine experience or humility, but on borrowed suffering. His identity becomes a kind of performance, dependent on taking from the lives of others and presenting their pain as his own.

The recurring images of Colorado irises, rain, and cracked cement create a sense of renewal and perpetual beginning. Irises bloom despite harsh conditions; rain refreshes what has been dry; cracked cement suggests that even in hard, damaged places, something living can emerge. These images point toward resilience. They imply that life continues to push through, that beauty can appear unexpectedly, and that beginnings are always possible, even after emotional ruin or disillusionment.

By the end, the speaker resolves to forget him. This forgetting is not passive but deliberate: the speaker mentally locks him away, containing his memory so that it can no longer intrude or exert power. Letting go becomes an act of self-preservation. In refusing to keep circling around his emptiness, the speaker reclaims attention, imagination, and inner freedom. The man may once have seemed powerful because of his performance, but the speaker ultimately recognizes that he is not worth carrying forward. Forgetting him becomes a way of choosing renewal over resentment and self-possession over his influence.
outputs.L4:
The poem presents a speaker who is trying to free herself from the corrosive effects of envy and resentment. At its center is a man who appears performative, self-important, and perhaps theatrical in his way of occupying the world. He seems to demand attention, and the speaker’s emotional struggle comes from the power he has held over her imagination. Rather than simply rejecting him outright, the poem traces the more complicated inward process of loosening his hold.

Memory plays an important role in this process. The speaker moves through recollection as if revisiting the emotional landscape in which her resentment first took root. These memories are not abstract; they are surrounded by vivid images of the natural world. Through this imagery, the poem contrasts the man’s artificial, self-conscious performance with a more authentic and renewing beauty found in nature. The natural images help the speaker recover a sense of perspective, reminding her that the world is larger, richer, and more alive than the figure who has occupied her thoughts.

The poem also uses the idea of imaginative containment. The speaker does not merely forget the man passively; she actively places him somewhere in the mind where he can no longer intrude. To “lock” him away is to reclaim control over her own attention and emotional life. This act suggests that forgetting is not a failure of memory, but a deliberate form of self-preservation. By enclosing him mentally, the speaker reduces his power and refuses to let him continue shaping her inner world.

Ultimately, the poem finds renewal in the decision to let go. Releasing envy and resentment allows the speaker to return to beauty, freedom, and agency. The act of forgetting becomes a kind of rebirth: once the man is contained and dismissed, the speaker can begin again. The poem therefore suggests that emotional liberation does not come from defeating the other person, but from withdrawing the energy once given to them. In choosing to forget, the speaker restores the possibility of perpetual beginnings.
outputs.L5:
Memories are strange things. They arrive when we least expect them: in the smell of rain, in an old song, in the quiet corner of a room we thought we had forgotten. Some memories warm us, reminding us of who we were and what we loved. Others return with weight, asking us to look again at what hurt, what changed, and what can never be the same.

Letting go does not mean erasing the past. It does not mean pretending something did not matter. Letting go means accepting that memories can live inside us without controlling where we go next. It means understanding that what happened is part of our story, but it is not the whole story.

What we carry shapes us, but what we release frees us. We learn, slowly, that holding on too tightly can keep us standing in the same place. And when we finally allow ourselves to move forward, the memories remain—not as chains, but as quiet reminders of how far we have come.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a contemporary free-verse poem about trying to let go of envy toward a pompous male writer, blending images of New York, Colorado irises, tropical plants, winter, music, and memory.
counterfactuals.output:
I keep trying to forgive him  
for standing in every room  
like a sentence already praised.

His laugh tilts back—  
a brass instrument  
polished by other people’s breath—  
and I, with my pocketful of drafts,  
feel the old green weather gather.

New York is no help.  
It teaches hunger in reflections:  
black windows, wet avenues,  
the Empire State blinking  
through steam like a cigarette  
someone famous abandoned mid-thought.

In cafés, I hear his name  
passed hand to hand  
like a warm coin.  
I stir my coffee  
until it becomes a small brown storm.

But memory, inconvenient florist,  
keeps opening other rooms.

Colorado irises  
beside a ditch in June—  
purple as bruised twilight,  
yellow throats bright  
with their foolish, holy trumpets.

My mother’s hands  
parting tropical leaves  
on a windowsill in winter:  
split-leaf philodendron, hibiscus,  
a palm pretending  
the snow outside was only paper.

How patiently the plants endured  
their borrowed climate,  
their radiators, their dim glass,  
their dream of rain.

Maybe envy is also a houseplant,  
root-bound, glossy,  
turning toward whatever light  
another person seems to own.

I have fed it too well.

Tonight the city is salted with cold.  
Taxis hiss through slush.  
Somewhere a saxophone climbs  
from the subway grate,  
not asking permission  
to be beautiful.

I think of the irises sleeping now  
under Colorado frost,  
their blue fire folded away  
like a letter I don’t need to send.

I think of all the music  
that survived without applause:  
my father humming off-key  
in the kitchen,  
radiators knocking in the dark,  
snow spelling nothing  
on the fire escape.

Let him have his velvet jacket,  
his gravity,  
his paragraphs arranged  
like expensive furniture.

I am tired  
of measuring my life  
against a man  
who mistakes echo for cathedral.

The winter loosens  
one silver thread at a time.  
Under the pavement,  
under the envy,  
something unrenowned is still alive.

I press my hand  
to the cold window.

Inside, the tropical leaves  
keep making their quiet arguments  
for green.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a surreal lyric poem in the first person that begins with “I am not saying ‘mark my words,’” and explores resentment, beauty, performance, poverty stories, and the desire to forget someone.
counterfactuals.output:
I am not saying ‘mark my words,’  
because the words have already been marked—  
bruised fruit in the bowl,  
blue fingerprints on the moon’s white throat.  

I am only saying I kept the receipts  
from every beautiful wound:  
the chandelier that wept sugar,  
the horse made of rain  
kneeling in the orchestra pit,  
your face applauding itself  
in every darkened window.  

I learned resentment as a costume,  
stitched from attic dust and borrowed teeth.  
I wore it onstage beneath the spotlight’s hot coin,  
smiled until the audience mistook me  
for a vase full of knives.  
How lovely, they said,  
how sharp she has become.  

I know the old poverty stories—  
the soup thinned with prayer,  
the mother folding hunger into napkins,  
the child sleeping in a coat  
while winter counted the ribs of the house.  
I have told them too,  
polished them like heirlooms,  
made them sing for strangers  
who wanted sorrow with their wine.  

But beauty is a dangerous employer.  
It pays in mirrors.  
It asks me to turn my grief  
so the light can enter it.  
It asks me to dance  
while my shoes fill with black water.  

And you—  
you stand in the velvet distance,  
a name I keep trying to misplace.  
I bury you under lilacs.  
You bloom.  
I feed you to the sea.  
You return as salt on my tongue.  
I burn your letters  
and the smoke learns my handwriting.  

I want to forget you  
the way a room forgets music  
after the piano is carried away.  
I want my mind rinsed clean,  
my dreams emptied of your weather,  
your cathedral of shoulders,  
your small, cruel halo  
hanging over the bread.  

Still, some nights  
I open my mouth  
and a flock of red birds escapes,  
each one calling your name  
as if it were bread,  
as if it were home,  
as if I had not spent my whole life  
being poor enough  
to cherish what hurt me.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate an experimental prose poem with fragmented sentences and vivid imagery: a thief in winter, a man preaching, a terrarium with huge leaves, stars over New York, irises in Colorado, and locking someone away in the mind.
counterfactuals.output:
The thief came in winter, all elbows and blue breath.  
Snow ticking at his cuffs. Pockets full of borrowed dusk.  

He stole nothing at first—  
only the warmth from the room,  
only the little animal of silence  
curled under the stove.

A man was preaching on the corner,  
his mouth a brass bell cracked by weather.  
Repent, he said, or remember.  
The city misheard him beautifully.  
Steam rose from grates like ghosts changing clothes.

Inside the terrarium: huge leaves.  
Glossy, prehistoric, veined with green lightning.  
A jungle reduced to glass and mist.  
Each leaf pressed its palm against the wall  
as if asking out.  
As if knowing the word exile.

Stars over New York—  
not many, but enough to accuse the rooftops.  
Pins in black velvet.  
Small burns above the taxis,  
above the bodegas and laundromats,  
above the thief’s shoulders  
as he carried winter through the avenues.

In Colorado, irises opened their purple throats.  
Blue flags in the wind.  
Petals like bruised silk,  
like messages from a country  
where the snow had finally forgiven the earth.

And you—  
I locked you away in the mind.  
Not a prison, exactly.  
A room behind a room behind a room.  
Wallpaper of old conversations.  
A chair facing no window.  
Your name folded into a drawer  
with the dull knives and dead batteries.

Sometimes you knock.

Sometimes the terrarium fogs from inside.

Sometimes the preacher lifts both hands  
and the stars fall quietly into his sleeves.

The thief keeps walking.  
Winter keeps inventing new doors.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a poem in the style of contemporary confessional poetry about releasing a toxic mentor or rival, using lush natural imagery, urban lights, violins, and the repeated idea of “letting go.”
counterfactuals.output:
I keep finding your voice in my mouth,  
a bitter seed tucked under the tongue,  
and I am tired of watering it.

For years I called it discipline—  
the way you trimmed me back,  
said bloom and meant bleed,  
said listen and meant kneel.

Even the city knew.  
At dusk, the windows lit one by one  
like small verdicts. Traffic loosened  
its red beads down the avenue.  
Somewhere above the laundromat,  
a violin practiced grief until it shone.

I stood there, carrying your name  
like a jar of hornets,  
my hands warm from the danger.

Letting go, I thought,  
would be a cliff, a dramatic sky,  
my body flung clean into weather.  
But it was smaller than that.

It was not answering.  
It was closing the book  
where your fingerprints had bruised the margins.  
It was walking past the old café  
with its gold lamps and rain-silvered chairs  
and not making a shrine of the table.

Letting go.  
The trees along the curb did it constantly—  
leaf after leaf, little green flames  
surrendering to the gutter’s dark river.  
No speech. No apology.  
Just autumn performing its ancient honesty.

And the violins kept rising  
from a window I could not see,  
thin as moonlight, stubborn as vines  
climbing a brick wall toward air.

I wanted you to witness  
how beautiful I became without you,  
which is to say  
I had not yet left.

So I opened my fist.

Out flew the wasps,  
out fell the rusted key,  
out spilled the rehearsed arguments  
glittering like broken glass under streetlights.

Letting go. Letting go.

My life did not become a meadow overnight.  
There were sirens. There was smoke.  
There were mornings I woke  
with your old commandments  
perched on my chest like crows.

But beneath them, something green  
kept insisting.

A fern uncurling in the alley crack.  
Rain polishing the black backs of taxis.  
The river, filthy and radiant,  
dragging every neon sign into its trembling body  
and carrying it away.

I am learning from water now.  
From the weed that splits concrete.  
From the violin string that survives  
by being tightened, yes,  
but sings only when it is touched  
by something gentler than a fist.

Letting go is not forgiveness.  
Not always. Not yet.

Sometimes it is simply  
refusing to build another room  
inside your shadow.

Tonight the city opens  
its thousand electric flowers.  
The sky bruises purple, then heals into black.  
I walk home alone,  
and the air tastes of rain, exhaust,  
and something almost like mercy.

Your voice calls once  
from the far end of memory.

I let it go.

I let it go.

I let it go,  
and my own voice returns—  
wild, wet, luminous—  
a violin in the dark  
teaching the dark  
how to tremble.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a dense, associative free verse piece about a self-important man who claims others’ suffering as his own, contrasted with the speaker finding beauty and renewal among plants, rain, cement, and flowers.
counterfactuals.output:
He arrives with a borrowed wound  
pinned to his lapel like a medal,  
mouth full of funerals he did not attend,  
naming himself the center of every ash.  

He says *my grief*  
and means the room should bow.  
He says *our pain*  
and pockets the pronoun.  
In his hands, even a stranger’s hunger  
becomes a mirror, polished, carried  
from table to table  
so everyone can admire  
how deeply he reflects.  

I leave him there,  
swelling in the stale light  
of his own importance,  
a dark bread rising  
without yeast,  
without offering.

Outside, rain begins its small republic  
on the sidewalk.  
Cement drinks, darkens, remembers  
it was once dust, stone, shell,  
something crushed  
and made useful.  

The weeds at the curb  
lift their green wrists.  
Moss writes quietly  
in the cracks,  
a soft alphabet no one has to own.  
Petunias bruise purple against the weather  
and do not call it tragedy.  
Marigolds burn on  
with their bitter, holy smell.  

I kneel near the gutter  
where petals collect  
like scraps of silk,  
where rainwater carries pollen, oil,  
one torn leaf,  
the silver tremble of a worm  
returning to earth.  

Here is suffering  
without performance:  
root split by stone,  
stem bent and rising,  
seed husk emptied  
of its one small body  
so the green blade can enter the world  
clean as a new question.  

Here is beauty  
not asking to be believed.  
The cement shining black.  
The rain stitching air to ground.  
The flowers opening  
their many soft mouths  
and saying nothing  
about deserving.  

I breathe with them,  
less important than mud,  
less lonely than before,  
my hands smelling of iron, water,  
crushed stems, beginnings.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
